name: Security Attribute
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Security as a Spectrum, Not a Switch: Blockchain's Security Attribute
lesson.summary: The security attribute measures whether a system resists a specified set of threats under specified assumptions, and in blockchain systems it depends on both cryptography and economic incentive design, since neither one alone is sufficient.
lesson.body:
Security is one of the quality attributes introduced earlier in this chapter, and like the others, it is not a single yes or no property. A system is never simply secure. It resists particular threats, made by attackers with particular resources and motivations, up to a particular cost, and stating security claims without naming those specifics is close to meaningless. This is true of software architecture generally, but blockchain systems make the point unusually vivid, because the field routinely uses the word security to describe two almost entirely different kinds of guarantees.

The first kind rests directly on cryptography, specifically encryption and related primitives like hashing and digital signatures. These tools give a blockchain confidentiality and integrity guarantees: a private key that has not been exposed cannot be forged, and a signed transaction cannot be altered without invalidating the signature. When someone loses funds because a private key was stolen through a phishing attack or a compromised exchange, that is a failure at the cryptographic layer, and better encryption practices, hardware wallets, multi-signature setups, would have prevented it.

The second kind of security has almost nothing to do with cryptography and everything to do with economics and game theory. A 51 percent attack, in which an entity gains control of a majority of a proof of work chain's mining power, does not break any encryption at all. Every signature still verifies correctly. What breaks is the assumption that no single party can economically afford to out-hash everyone else combined, an assumption that holds only as long as acquiring that much hashing power costs more than the attacker could profit from double spending or extorting the network. This is why serious analysis of consensus security expresses it in dollar terms, the cost to mount an attack, rather than in cryptographic terms alone, because cryptography was never the layer under threat.

These two failure modes call for entirely different mitigations, which is exactly why treating security as a single attribute to be maximized is a mistake. Hardening cryptography, larger keys, better signature schemes, better custody practices, does nothing to raise the cost of a 51 percent attack. Raising the cost of a consensus attack, through more distributed mining, more total staked capital, or a larger validator set, does nothing to stop a user from having their private key phished. A complete security posture has to address both layers, and a team that only thinks about encryption because that is the part of security they know how to reason about will leave the economic layer wide open.

This is also why security, like every other quality attribute discussed in this chapter, only becomes actionable once it is broken into specific scenarios the way a utility tree demands. Instead of asking whether the system is secure, the useful question is: secure against an attacker willing to spend how much money, targeting which layer, over what time horizon. A security attribute stated that specifically can be tested, budgeted for, and honestly compared across different architectural choices, which a vague assurance never can.
